(3) To obtain a W 0 W_{0} that will produce low ℒ ⁡ ( W 0 , X ) \mathcal{L}(W_{0};X) at test time, the most direct approach is to optimize the same loss at training time over a large training set of sequences on average. This direct approach is an example of End-to-End (E2E) training, where the training loss matches the test loss. When TTT uses a W 0 W_{0} trained in this fashion, we call it TTT-E2E . As a contrasting example, consider another approach that naively imitates the training loss of a static model without taking into account that W 0 W_{0} will be updated at test time: ℒ naive ​ ( W 0 , X ) = 1 T ​ ∑ t = 1 T ℓ t ​ ( W 0 ) . \mathcal{L}_{\texttt{naive}}(W_{0};X)=\frac{1}{T}\sumop\displaylimits_{t=1}^{T}\ell_{t}(W_{0}). (4) This approach is not E2E, since there is a mismatch between the model’s behavior at training and test time. As a consequence, we can provide little guarantee that a minimizer of ℒ naive \mathcal{L}_{\texttt{naive}} will also produce low test loss ℒ \mathcal{L} . We call this approach TTT-naive . It has been the mainstream approach in the literature of dynamic evaluation [ 72 , 60 ] . The right panel of Figure 2 plots the token-level test loss ℓ t \ell_{t} , averaged over many test sequences, for t = 1 , … , 128 t=1,\dots,128 . So far, we have discussed four methods: Transformer with full attention (orange), our toy baseline without attention (green), TTT-naive (gray), and TTT-E2E (blue for b = 1 b=1 ; we will cover the variant with b = 16 b=16 in Subsection 2.3 ); see details of the experimental setup in Appendix A . While TTT-naive performs only slightly better than the toy baseline, TTT-E2E performs almost as well as full attention. In particular, TTT-E2E can effectively use more context to better predict the next token, as demonstrated by the test loss decreasing over time. For gradient-based optimization, computing ∇ ℒ ​ ( W 0 ) \nabla\mathcal{L}(W_{0}) for the E2E ℒ \mathcal{L} entails computing gradients of gradients, since the update rule in Equation 2 itself contains a gradient operation. Fortunately, modern frameworks for automatic differentiation can efficiently compute gradients of gradients with minimal overhead [ 13 , 25 ] . Once ∇ ℒ ​ ( W 0 ) \nabla\mathcal{L}(W_{0}) is computed, we can plug it into standard optimizers. In the field of meta-learning, gradient steps on ℒ \mathcal{L} are called the outer loop , and on ℓ \ell the inner loop . The current version of TTT-E2E still has two problems for large models in long context. The first is efficiency, because our inner loop has many steps that cannot be parallelized. The second is stability, because each gradient step in the inner loop depends on only a single token, which can easily lead to gradient explosion by chance. The next subsection addresses these two problems.

Preliminaries. End-to-end self-driving methods seek to obtain a policy, denoted as π \pi , that directly outputs driving decisions, such as desired trajectories 𝐭 \mathbf{t} , based on sensor inputs 𝐱 \mathbf{x} and a navigation command 𝐜 \mathbf{c} . Trajectories are of the form 𝐭 ~ = ( 𝐩 0 , 𝐩 1 , ⋯ , 𝐩 N ) \tilde{\mathbf{t}}=(\mathbf{p}_{0},\mathbf{p}_{1},\cdots,\mathbf{p}_{N}) , which is a sequence of waypoints. These are Bird’s Eye View (BEV) positions of the vehicle over N N evenly spaced time steps. The policy estimates trajectories from sensor inputs 𝐱 0 \mathbf{x}_{0} (such as camera images), and a discrete navigation command 𝐜 0 \mathbf{c}_{0} (indicating driver intention in ambiguous situations, e.g. left/ right/ straight), captured at the current time step, indexed with 0 0 . Among the existing paradigms for end-to-end driving, the straightforward approach of regressing trajectories using a dataset of human driving demonstrations can be referred to as trajectory regression. While our approach is compatible with trajectory regression, in the following, we primarily address its application to a new emerging paradigm with higher performance in the recent literature: trajectory scoring (e.g. , Hydra-MDP [ 33 ] , VADv2 [ 5 ] and RAD [ 12 ] ). We discuss the methodology and results for applying our approach to trajectory regression methods such as UniAD [ 22 ] and TransFuser [ 7 ] in the supplementary material. Trajectory Scoring. In this formulation, the planner outputs a set of scalar ‘score features’ { s j } j = 1 k \{s_{j}\}_{j=1}^{k} for a ‘planning vocabulary’ of k k different trajectories. The score features numerically capture different aspects of desired driving behavior, such as avoiding collisions and making progress. These features can then be aggregated into a single final score via an aggregation function ϕ \phi . During inference, the trajectory with the largest predicted final score is selected: { s j } j = 1 k = { π θ ​ ( 𝐭 j , 𝐱 0 , 𝐜 0 ) } j = 1 k , \{s_{j}\}_{j=1}^{k}=\{\pi_{\theta}(\mathbf{t}_{j},\mathbf{x}_{0},\mathbf{c}_{0})\}_{j=1}^{k}, (1) 𝐭 ^ 0 = arg ⁡ max 𝐭 j ​ { ϕ ⁡ ( s j ) } j = 1 k . \hat{\mathbf{t}}_{0}=\underset{\mathbf{t}_{j}}{\arg\max}\{\phi(s_{j})\}_{j=1}^{k}. (2) As a result of this design, the planner is inherently multi-modal, with the distribution of scores over the planning vocabulary providing a way to represent planning uncertainty. For this type of planner, learning the policy’s parameters θ \theta can be formulated as: arg ⁡ min θ ​ 𝔼 ( 𝐭 , 𝐱 , 𝐜 ) ∼ D k ​ d ​ [ ℒ k ​ d ​ ( e ⁡ ( 𝐭 , 𝐱 , 𝐜 ) , π θ ​ ( 𝐭 , 𝐱 , 𝐜 ) ) ] , \arg\min_{\theta}\mathbb{E}_{(\mathbf{t},\mathbf{x},\mathbf{c})\sim D_{kd}}[\mathcal{L}_{kd}(e(\mathbf{t},\mathbf{x},\mathbf{c}),\pi_{\theta}(\mathbf{t},\mathbf{x},\mathbf{c}))], (3) where e e is an expert algorithm that can provide ground truth score features for any sampled trajectory, and D k ​ d = { ( 𝐭 , 𝐱 , 𝐜 ) , ⋯ } D_{kd}=\{(\mathbf{t},\mathbf{x},\mathbf{c}),\cdots\} is a knowledge distillation dataset generated by sampling this expert algorithm for different inputs, typically in a driving simulator [ 2 , 11 ] or world model [ 61 , 14 ] . In practice, the score features are normalized to the range ( 0 , 1 ) (0,1) , and ℒ k ​ d \mathcal{L}_{kd} is implemented as a cross-entropy loss. 2.1 Cluster Entropy In essence, the scoring procedure from Eq. ( 1 ) and Eq. ( 2 ) acts as a classifier over the k k classes in the planning vocabulary. We formulate a new uncertainty measure, Cluster Entropy, to translate this intuition into an unsupervised training objective for end-to-end planning, which does not require an expert algorithm as in Eq. ( 3 ). Our key challenge is that the planning vocabulary k k is often very large, typically encompassing several thousands of possible trajectories. Therefore, even for simple driving scenarios, several neighboring trajectories in the vocabulary will result in nearly identical scores. Simply minimizing the entropy in the distribution over scores over would result in an objective that encourages the model to avoid trajectories that have a larger number of nearby neighbors in the vocabulary, e.g. , driving straight. Therefore, such a naive entropy is unsuitable for uncertainty estimation in this setting. Trajectory Candidates. To tackle this, we first sample a set of M M trajectory candidates { 𝐭 m } m = 1 M \{\mathbf{t}_{m}\}_{m=1}^{M} from the planning vocabulary, where M << k M<<k . We use a weighted sampling process which prioritizes candidates that have a high average score on the test set as per the expert algorithm e e . Additional details regarding this procedure are provided in the supplementary material. While the entropy over this reduced set of M M scores already serves as a meaningful uncertainty measure, as evidenced by our experiments, we now aim to further improve its effectiveness and interpretability. Direction-based Sampling. Next, we use domain-specific criteria to select trajectory anchors from the M M trajectory candidates. Following [ 50 ] , we select 5 anchors ( sharp left , slight left , forward , slight right , sharp right ). sharp left/right , the candidates with the largest lateral offsets, are selected first. slight left/right are the candidates with lateral offsets closest to half that of sharp left/right , and forward is the trajectory with the smallest lateral offset. Score Aggregation. As shown in Fig. 2 (top), we aim to construct a 5-way categorical distribution capturing the distribution of predicted scores over the 5 driving directions. For this, we construct 5 clusters by identifying the nearest anchor to each of the M M candidates in terms of L 2 L_{2} distance. In each resulting cluster, we add up the predicted scores for all trajectories to obtain an anchor score s ​ c ​ o ​ r ​ e a score_{a} . We compute a probability distribution via normalization ( s ​ c ​ o ​ r ​ e a ∑ a = 1 5 s ​ c ​ o ​ r ​ e a \frac{score_{a}}{\sum_{a=1}^{5}score_{a}} ), and define Cluster Entropy (denoted as H H ) to be the Shannon Entropy of this distribution. 2.2 Test-Time Training (TTT) Equipped with our unsupervised training objective, our goal is to minimize test-time uncertainty, which is the key idea of TTT approaches in the literature. We follow the standard practice of performing a single step of gradient descent to update our network’s parameters θ \theta [ 13 ] . We use the Cluster Entropy H ⁡ ( 𝐱 ) H(\mathbf{x}) as an objective function to optimize. Specifically, given H ⁡ ( 𝐱 ) H(\mathbf{x}) calculated following a forward pass through π θ \pi_{\theta} , we obtain the gradient ∂ H ∂ θ \frac{\partial H}{\partial\theta} by backpropagation. However, instead of directly updating θ \theta with the calculated gradient, we store ∂ H ∂ θ \frac{\partial H}{\partial\theta} in a buffer of length F = 4 F=4 , as shown in Fig. 2 (bottom). At time-step i i , we update the network using the average of all gradients { ∂ H ∂ θ } a ​ v ​ g \{\frac{\partial H}{\partial\theta}\}_{avg} currently in our buffer, obtaining θ ^ i = θ − η ​ { ∂ H ∂ θ } a ​ v ​ g \hat{\theta}_{i}=\theta-\eta\{\frac{\partial H}{\partial\theta}\}_{avg} , where η \eta is the learning rate. Intuitively, this suppresses the model’s ability to assign high scores in multiple clusters. This, in turn, corrects the scores of outlier predictions that vary significantly from other trajectories in their cluster. Deployment. Note that the gradient calculated at time-step i i only uses gradients of historical time-steps already present in the buffer. Therefore, beyond the smoothness provided by gradient averaging, our use of a buffer enables asynchronous and parallel execution. During deployment, the gradient calculation process can be executed on independent computational hardware, so that the more critical inference process holds a minimal overhead in latency.
